sections.title: What is Framing?
sections.content: Framing is the way information is presented, which influences how people interpret it. The same fact framed differently can produce opposite reactions. '95% fat-free' sounds healthier than '5% fat' — same fact, different frame.
bullets: Framing changes perception without changing facts
Positive frames ('save lives') are more persuasive than negative ones ('let people die')
Emotional frames are more memorable than neutral ones

sections.title: The Priming Effect
sections.content: Priming occurs when exposure to one stimulus influences response to a subsequent stimulus. In debate, the order and framing of your arguments can prime the judge to view later arguments more favorably.
bullets: Priming activates certain associations in the listener's mind
Setting the frame early gives you control over how arguments are evaluated
Example: Framing a tax debate as 'fairness' primes the judge to evaluate based on fairness

sections.instruction: Which headline uses framing to create a more negative impression?
options: '4% of workers still jobless despite recovery'
sections.feedback: '4% of workers still jobless' frames the same statistic negatively.

sections.q: In debate, why is it important to set the framing early?
options: It controls how the judge evaluates subsequent arguments
sections.explain: Early framing sets the lens through which everything else is viewed. The side that controls the frame often wins.

sections.sentence: {0} occurs when exposure to one idea influences how you respond to a later idea.
sections.feedback: Priming activates associations that shape later responses.

sections.statement: Framing changes the underlying facts of an argument.
sections.feedback: Framing changes the presentation and perception, not the facts themselves.

sections.instruction: What type of cognitive effect is being demonstrated here?
sections.argument: Before a debate on healthcare, the first speaker says: 'Today we must decide whether healthcare is a human right or a privilege for those who can afford it.' The entire debate then focuses on whether healthcare is a right, ignoring alternative funding models entirely.
options: Framing effect — the speaker set the lens through which the debate would be evaluated
sections.feedback: By framing the choice as 'right vs. privilege,' the speaker controlled the entire debate's frame. That is framing at work.

questions.q: How can a debater use framing strategically?
options: By choosing words and context that make their arguments appear more favorable
questions.feedback: Strategic framing selects the lens through which you want the judge to evaluate arguments.
